title: Passover night (Exodus 12:1–14)
hook: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste, and the angel passes over

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plagues, and a king whose every no made the next one easier. Your line was a hard heart gets harder. Where did you pause before an automatic no? Day three hundred eighty-six.

Some meals are just meals. Others you can describe years later: who sat where, what was said, what the room smelled like. A last dinner before someone moved away. The table the night before a wedding, or after a funeral. Exodus is about to describe a meal like that, the night before everything changes. Nine plagues have struck Egypt. One more is coming, the worst of all, the death of the firstborn. And before it falls, God gives Moses and Aaron instructions. Not for a battle. For dinner.
screen: `SOME MEALS YOU REMEMBER.` → `ONE PLAGUE LEFT.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FOR DINNER.`

segments.voice: Each household is to take a lamb, a young male without blemish. Keep it a few days. Then, at twilight, kill it, and put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door frame of the house. Roast it whole and eat it that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. And eat it dressed for travel, in the King James Bible: "with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD's passover." Shoes on. Ready to walk out the door. Then the promise: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." That's the word. Pesach in Hebrew, Passover in English. The plague will pass over the marked houses. And then, before any of it has happened, God says this night must be remembered: "this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast." A feast of remembering, commanded before the event even begins. Jewish families have kept it ever since. At the Passover Seder, children ask why this night is different from all other nights, and the story is told again at the table. Christians carry this night too. The Gospels set Jesus's last supper and his death at Passover time, and Paul writes, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." That is why in many languages the word for Easter comes from Pesach: Pascha. Readers of every tradition also feel the weight of this night. The deliverance of one people came with grief in the houses of another, and Jewish tradition has long refused to celebrate it carelessly.
screen: `A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH.` · `BLOOD ON THE DOORPOSTS.` · `SHOES ON, STAFF IN HAND.` · `PESACH, PASCHA, EASTER.` · then, large: `WHEN I SEE THE BLOOD, I WILL PASS OVER YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something standing, remembering. Take a cracker, a piece of bread, a sip of water, whatever is near. Stand up if you can. Hold it for a moment. Think of a night in your own life that changed everything, or the story of someone who came before you and got out of something hard. Eat slowly, standing, shoes on, as if you might have to leave. If you pray, you can give thanks for deliverance. If you don't, simply remember. The bell holds the time.
Passover. Pesach in Hebrew: the night the plague passed over the houses marked with the lamb's blood, kept as a feast of remembering ever since.
Your line: remember this night. Today, tell someone younger one story from your family's past that they've never heard. Day three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish families keep Passover each spring with the Seder meal and the retelling of the Exodus; Christians celebrate Easter as their Pascha, and many churches read Exodus 12 on Holy Thursday, the evening they remember the Last Supper.

original.note: Hebrew: Passover, from the verb to pass over or spare. the root of the Greek Pascha.

trapdoor: what you thought: Passover is a Jewish holiday that comes around Easter.
what it means: a meal eaten in haste on the night of deliverance, commanded to be remembered forever, and kept by Jews to this day.

what a scholar hears: Pesach became Greek Pascha, which gave the word for Easter in many languages; the Gospels date Jesus's death by Passover, though John and the other Gospels place the meal on slightly different days.

notes: The Seder's 'why is this night different' (the Four Questions) is described, not quoted.

The death of the firstborn is mentioned with care; the closing line about Jewish tradition refusing to celebrate carelessly alludes to customs such as removing drops of wine and the midrash of God rebuking the angels. Confirm phrasing.
Synoptic vs Johannine dating of the Last Supper/crucifixion mentioned briefly in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Pascha as the source of Easter's name in many languages (Pâques, Pascua, Pasqua, Greek Pascha). Confirm.
howItsDone: Exodus 12 is the first reading at the Holy Thursday Mass of the Lord's Supper in the Catholic lectionary and in several other liturgical churches. Confirm.
